section.heading: 10.2. Calculus with Parametric Curves
section.paragraph: Having seen how to represent curves by parametric equations, we now apply the methods of calculus to these parametric curves. In particular, we solve problems involving tangents, areas, arc length, speed, and surface area.
section.heading: Tangents
section.paragraph: Suppose $$f$$ and $$g$$ are differentiable functions and we want to find the tangent line at a point on the parametric curve $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , where $$y$$ is also a differentiable function of $$x$$ . Then the Chain Rule gives
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \cdot \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}$$
If $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ , we can solve for $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ :
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}}}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} \text{if} \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \neq 0$$

If we think of the curve as being traced out by a moving particle, then $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}$$ and $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}$$ are the vertical and horizontal velocities of the particle and Formula 1 says that the slope of the tangent is the ratio of these velocities.

Equation 1 (which you can remember by thinking of canceling the $$\mathit{dt}$$ ’s) enables us to find the slope $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ of the tangent to a parametric curve without having to eliminate the parameter $$t$$ . We see from (1) that the curve has a horizontal tangent when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , provided that $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ , and it has a vertical tangent when $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , provided that $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ . (If both $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ and $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ , then we would need to use other methods to determine the slope of the tangent.) This information is useful for sketching parametric curves.
As we have learned, it is also often useful to consider $$d^{2}y/dx^{2}$$ . This can be found by replacing $$y$$ by $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}$$ in Equation 1:
$$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right) = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}}$$
Note that $$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \neq \frac{\frac{d^{2}y}{dt^{2}}}{\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: A curve $$C$$ is defined by the parametric equations $$x = t^{2}$$ , $$y = t^{3} - 3t$$ .

list.item: (a) Show that $$C$$ has two tangents at the point $$(3,0)$$ and find their equations.
(b) Find the points on $$C$$ where the tangent is horizontal or vertical.
(c) Determine where the curve is concave upward or downward.

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) Notice that $$x = 3$$ for $$t = \pm \sqrt{3}$$ and, in both cases, $$y = t({t^{2} - 3}) = 0$$ . Therefore the point $$(3,0)$$ on $$C$$ arises from two values of the parameter, $$t = \sqrt{3}$$ and $$t = - \sqrt{3}$$ . This indicates that $$C$$ crosses itself at $$(3,0)$$ . Since $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}}{\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}} = \frac{3t^{2} - 3}{2t}$$ the slope of the tangent when $$t = \sqrt{3}$$ is $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 6/(2\sqrt{3}) = \sqrt{3}$$ , and when $$t = - \sqrt{3}$$ the slope is $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = - 6/(2\sqrt{3}) = - \sqrt{3}$$ . Thus we have two different tangent lines at $$(3,0)$$ with equations $$y = \sqrt{3}{({x - 3})}$$ and $$y = - \sqrt{3}{({x - 3})}$$

(b) $$C$$ has a horizontal tangent when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 0$$ , that is, when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 0$$ and $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ . Since $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = 3t^{2} - 3$$ , this happens when $$t^{2} = 1$$ , that is, $$t = \pm 1$$ . The corresponding points on $$C$$ are $$(1, - 2)$$ and $$(1,2)$$ . $$C$$ has a vertical tangent when $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 2t = 0$$ , that is, $$t = 0$$ . (Note that $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} \neq 0$$ there.) The corresponding point on $$C$$ is $$(0,0)$$ .

(c) To determine concavity we calculate the second derivative: $$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{3t^{2} - 3}{2t} \right)}{\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}} = \frac{\frac{6t^{2} + 6}{4t^{2}}}{2t} = \frac{3t^{2} + 3}{4t^{3}}$$ Thus the curve is concave upward when $$t > 0$$ and concave downward when $$t < 0$$ .

(d) Using the information from parts (b) and (c), we sketch $$C$$ in Figure 1. Figure 1 Details A curve with a loop and four lines are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. Arrows are placed on the curve indicating the direction of the path it takes. The curve enters from the bottom right corner, goes up to the left, crosses the positive x-axis at (3, 0), goes up to the left, reaches a high point at (1, 2), descends downward, bulging to the left, touching the origin, reaches a low point at (1, negative 2), goes up to the right, crosses the x-axis again at (3, 0), and exits at the top right corner. The first line, labeled y = negative sqrt(3) (x minus 3) is tangent to the curve at (3, 0) as it climbs upward to the left. The second line labeled y = sqrt(3) (x minus 3) is tangent to the curve at (3, 0) as it climbs upward to the right. The third line, labeled t = 1 is tangent to the curve at its low point, (1, negative 2). The fourth line, labeled t = negative 1 is tangent to the curve at its high point, (1, 2).

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: (a) Find the tangent to the cycloid $$x = r(\theta - \sin\theta)$$ , $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ at the point where $$\theta = \pi/3$$ . (See Example 10.1.9.)
(b) At what points is the tangent horizontal? When is it vertical?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The slope of the tangent line is $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{r\sin\theta}{r(1 - \cos\theta)} = \frac{\sin\theta}{1 - \cos\theta}$$ When $$\theta = \pi/3$$ , we have $$x = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{3} - \sin\frac{\pi}{3}} \right) = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{3} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right) y = r\left( {1 - \cos\frac{\pi}{3}} \right) = \frac{r}{2}$$ and $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\sin\left( {\pi/3} \right)}{1 - \cos\left( {\pi/3} \right)} = \frac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1 - \frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{3}$$ Therefore the slope of the tangent is $$\sqrt{3}$$ and its equation is $$y - \frac{r}{2} = \sqrt{3}\left( {x - \frac{r\pi}{3} + \frac{r\sqrt{3}}{2}} \right)$$ or $$\sqrt{3}x - y = r\left( {\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} - 2} \right)$$ The tangent is sketched in Figure 2. Figure 2 Details A cycloid and 10 lines tangent to it is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis is displayed from negative 2 pi r to 6 pi r in increments of 2 pi r. Each arch of the cycloid has a width of 2 pi r. Five vertical lines are tangent to the cycloid at the points it touches the x-axis, namely, (negative 2 pi r, 0), (0, 0), (2 pi r, 0), (4 pi r, 0), and (6 pi r, 0). Four horizontal lines are tangent to the cycloid at the top most point of each arch, namely, (negative pi r, 2 r), (pi r, 2 r), (3 pi r, 2 r), and (5 pi r, 2 r). A line sloping upward to the right is tangent to the cycloid at a point labeled theta = pi/3, located on the cycloid as it rises upward to the right from the origin.

(b) The tangent is horizontal when $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx} = 0$$ , which occurs when $$\sin\theta = 0$$ and $$1 - \cos\theta \neq 0$$ , that is, $$\theta = (2n - 1)\pi$$ , $$n$$ an integer. The corresponding point on the cycloid is $$\left( (2n - 1)\pi r,2r \right)$$ . When $$\theta = 2n\pi$$ , both $$dx/d\theta$$ and $$dy/d\theta$$ are $$0$$ . It appears from the graph that there are vertical tangents at those points. We can verify this by using l’Hospital’s Rule as follows: $$\lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1 - \cos\theta} = \lim\limits_{\theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{+}}\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \infty$$ A similar computation shows that $$\left. \mathit{dy}/\mathit{dx}\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ as $$\left. \theta\rightarrow 2n\pi^{-} \right.$$ , so indeed there are vertical tangents when $$\theta = 2n\pi$$ , that is, when $$x = 2n\pi r$$ . (See Figure 2.)

section.heading: Areas
section.paragraph: We know that the area under a curve $$y = F(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ is $$A = {\int_{a}^{b}{F(x)dx}}$$ , where $$F(x) \geqslant 0$$ . If the curve is traced out once by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , then we can calculate an area formula by using the Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals as follows:
$$A = \int_{a}^{b}ydx = \int_{\alpha}^{\beta}g(t)f^{\prime}(t)dt \left\lbrack {or} \int_{\beta}^{\alpha}g(t)f^{\prime}(t)dt \right\rbrack$$
The limits of integration for $$t$$ are found as usual with the Substitution Rule. When $$x = a$$ , $$t$$ is either $$\alpha$$ or $$\beta$$ . When $$x = b$$ , $$t$$ is the remaining value.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the area under one arch of the cycloid
$$x = r(\theta - \sin\theta) y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$

image.alt: Details A cycloid is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis is displayed from 0 to 2 pi r in increments of 2 pi r. The cycloid enters from the top left, goes down to the right, meets the x-axis at the origin, goes up to the right and then down to meet the x-axis at (2 pi r, 0), goes up to the right, and exits at the top right of the viewing window. The area under one full arch between x = 0 and x = 2 pi r is shaded.

example.paragraph: Solution One arch of the cycloid (shown in Figure 3) is given by $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using the Substitution Rule with $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ and $$dx = r(1 - \cos\theta)d\theta$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = \int_{0}^{2\pi r}ydx = \int_{0}^{2\pi}r(1 - \cos\theta)r(1 - \cos\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}{(1 - \cos\theta)}^{2}d\theta = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}(1 - 2\cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta)d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack {1 - 2\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)} \right\rbrack d\theta} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{3}{2}\theta - 2\sin\theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ {\phantom{A} = r^{2}\left( \frac{3}{2} \cdot 2\pi \right) = 3\pi r^{2}} \end{array}$$

The result of Example 3 says that the area under one arch of the cycloid is three times the area of the rolling circle that generates the cycloid (see Example 10.1.9). Galileo guessed this result but it was first proved by the French mathematician Roberval and the Italian mathematician Torricelli.

section.heading: Arc Length
section.paragraph: We already know how to find the length $$L$$ of a curve $$C$$ given in the form $$y = F(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Formula 8.1.3 says that if $$F^{\prime}$$ is continuous, then
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)^{2}}dx}}$$

Suppose that $$C$$ can also be described by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ and $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = f^{\prime}(t) > 0$$ . This means that $$C$$ is traversed once, from left to right, as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ and $$f(\alpha) = a$$ , $$f(\beta) = b$$ . Putting Formula 1 into Formula 2 and using the Substitution Rule, we obtain

$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt}}{\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}\frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}}dt}}$$
Since $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} > 0$$ , we have
$$L = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}dt}$$

Even if $$C$$ can’t be expressed in the form $$y = F(x)$$ , Formula 3 is still valid but we obtain it by polygonal approximations. We divide the parameter interval $$\left\lbrack {\alpha,\beta} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals of equal width $$\Delta t$$ . If $$t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},\ldots,t_{n}$$ are the endpoints of these subintervals, then $$x_{i} = f(t_{i})$$ and $$y_{i} = g(t_{i})$$ are the coordinates of points $$P_{i}(x_{i},y_{i})$$ that lie on $$C$$ and the polygonal path with vertices $$P_{0},P_{1},\ldots,P_{n}$$ approximates $$C$$ . (See Figure 4.)

image.alt: Details A curve, twelve points, and eleven line segments are graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, labeled C, begins at a point labeled P_0, rises upward bulging to the left, passing through the points P_1 and P_2, runs horizontally to the right, bulging upward, passing through an unlabeled point, P_(i minus 1), and P_i, and then the curve descends downward bulging steeply slightly up and to the left, passing through five unlabeled points and ending at a point labeled P_n. Eleven line segments connect the first point on the curve to the second, the second point of the curve to the third, and so on.

section.paragraph: As in Section 8.1, we define the length $$L$$ of $$C$$ to be the limit of the lengths of these approximating polygonal paths as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ :
$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}\left| {P_{i - 1}P_{i}} \right|$$
The Mean Value Theorem, when applied to $$f$$ on the interval $$\lbrack{t_{i - 1},t_{i}}\rbrack$$ , gives a number $$t_{i}^{*}$$ in $$({t_{i - 1},t_{i}})$$ such that
Let $$\Delta x_{i} = x_{i} - x_{i - 1}$$ and $$\Delta y_{i} = y_{i} - y_{i - 1}$$ . Then the preceding equation becomes
$$\Delta x_{i} = f^{\prime}(t_{i}^{*})\Delta t$$
Similarly, when applied to $$g$$ , the Mean Value Theorem gives a number $$t_{i}^{\ast \ast}$$ in $$({t_{i - 1},t_{i}})$$ such that
$$\Delta y_{i} = g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{\ast \ast})\Delta t$$
Therefore

$$\begin{matrix} {|{P_{i - 1}P_{i}}| = {\sqrt{{({\Delta x_{i}})}^{2} + {({\Delta y_{i}})}^{2}} = \sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})\Delta t}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})\Delta t}\rbrack}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{|{P_{i - 1}P_{i}}|} = {\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta t}} \end{matrix}$$
and so
$$L = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\underset{i=1}{\overset{n}{\sum}}{\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t_{i}^{*})}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t_{i}^{**})}\rbrack}^{2}}\Delta t}$$

The sum in (4) resembles a Riemann sum for the function $$\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t)}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack}^{2}}$$ but it is not exactly a Riemann sum because $$t_{i}^{*} \neq t_{i}^{**}$$ in general. Nevertheless, if $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, it can be shown that the limit in (4) is the same as if $$t_{i}^{*}$$ and $$t_{i}^{**}$$ were equal, namely,
$$L = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\sqrt{{\lbrack{{f^{\prime}}(t)}\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack{g^{\prime}(t)}\rbrack}^{2}}dt}}$$
Thus, using Leibniz notation, we have the following result, which has the same form as Formula 3.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If a curve $$C$$ is described by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous on $$\lbrack\alpha,\beta\rbrack$$ and $$C$$ is traversed exactly once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ , then the length of $$C$$ is

section.paragraph: Notice that the formula in Theorem 5 is consistent with the general formula $$L = {\int{ds}}$$ of Section 8.1, where
$$\mathit{ds} = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}\mathit{dt}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If we use the representation of the unit circle given in Example 10.1.2,
$$x = \cos t y = \sin t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$
then $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = - \sin t$$ and $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = \cos t$$ , so Theorem 5 gives

$$L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t}dt}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt}} = 2\pi$$
as expected. If, on the other hand, we use the representation given in Example 10.1.3,
$$x = \sin 2t y = \cos 2t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$
then $$\mathit{dx}/\mathit{dt} = 2\cos 2t$$ , $$\mathit{dy}/\mathit{dt} = - 2\sin 2t$$ , and the integral in Theorem 5 gives

$${\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sqrt{4\cos^{2}(2t) + 4\sin^{2}(2t)}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{2dt}} = 4\pi$$

Notice that the integral gives twice the arc length of the circle because as $$t$$ increases from $$0$$ to $$2\pi$$ , the point $$\left( \sin 2t,\cos 2t \right)$$ traverses the circle twice. In general, when finding the length of a curve $$C$$ from a parametric representation, we have to be careful to ensure that $$C$$ is traversed only once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the length of one arch of the cycloid $$x = r\left( \theta - \sin\theta \right)$$ , $$y = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$ .
Solution From Example 3 we see that one arch is described by the parameter interval $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Since
$$\frac{dx}{d\theta} = r(1 - \cos\theta)$$
and
$$\frac{dy}{d\theta} = r\sin\theta$$
we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {L = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{dy}{d\theta} \right)^{2}}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2}{({1 - \cos\theta})}^{2} + r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{r^{2}({1 - 2\cos\theta + \cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta})}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{L} = r{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sqrt{2({1 - \cos\theta})}d\theta}}} \end{array}$$

To evaluate this integral we use the identity $$\sin^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}{({1 - \cos 2x})}$$ with $$\theta = 2x$$ , which gives $$1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^{2}(\theta/2)$$ . Since $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , we have $$0 \leqslant \theta/2 \leqslant \pi$$ and so $$\sin(\theta/2) \geqslant 0$$ . Therefore
$$\sqrt{2(1 - \cos\theta)} = \sqrt{4\sin^{2}(\theta/2)} = 2\left| {\sin(\theta/2)} \right| = 2\sin(\theta/2)$$
and so
$$\begin{array}{l} {L = 2r{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin(\theta/2)d\theta}} = 2r{\lbrack{- 2\cos(\theta/2)}\rbrack}_{0}^{2\pi}} \\ {\phantom{L} = 2r\lbrack 2 + 2\rbrack = 8r} \end{array}$$

The result of Example 5 says that the length of one arch of a cycloid is eight times the radius of the generating circle (see Figure 5). This was first proved in 1658 by Sir Christopher Wren, who later became the architect of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London.

image.alt: Details An arch and a circle are graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The arch, labeled L = 8 r, begins at the origin and ends at (2 pi, 0) on the x-axis. A circle is drawn such that its bottom-most point touches the x-axis and its top left portion is cut by the left leg of the arch. The radius of the circle is labeled r.

section.paragraph: The arc length function and speed

Recall that the arc length function (Formula 8.1.5) gives the length of a curve from an initial point to any other point on the curve. For a parametric curve $$C$$ given by $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ and $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, we let $$s(t)$$ be the arc length along $$C$$ from an initial point $$(f(\alpha),g(\alpha))$$ to a point $$(f(t),g(t))$$ on $$C$$ . By Theorem 5, the arc length function $$s$$ for parametric curves is
$$s(t) = {\int_{\alpha}^{t}{\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{du}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{du}} \right)^{2}}du}}$$
(We have replaced the variable of integration by $$u$$ so that $$t$$ does not have two meanings.)

If parametric equations describe the position of a moving particle (with $$t$$ representing time), then the speed of the particle at time $$t$$ , $$v(t)$$ , is the rate of change of distance traveled (arc length) with respect to time: $$s^{\prime}(t)$$ . By Equation 7 and Part 1 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have
$$v(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The position of a particle at time $$t$$ is given by the parametric equations $$x = 2t + 3$$ , $$y = 4t^{2}$$ , $$t \geq 0$$ . Find the speed of the particle when it is at the point $$(5,4)$$ .
Solution By Equation 8, the speed of the particle at any time $$t$$ is

The particle is at the point $$(5,4)$$ when $$t = 1$$ , so its speed at that point is $$v(1) = 2\sqrt{17} \approx 8.25.$$ . (If distance is measured in meters and time in seconds, then the speed is approximately $$8.25m/s$$ .)

section.heading: Surface Area
section.paragraph: In the same way as for arc length, we can adapt Formula 8.2.5 to obtain a formula for surface area. Suppose a curve $$C$$ is given by the parametric equations $$x = f(t)$$ , $$y = g(t)$$ , $$\alpha \leqslant t \leqslant \beta$$ , where $$f^{\prime}$$ , $$g^{\prime}$$ are continuous, $$g(t) \geqslant 0$$ , and $$C$$ is traversed exactly once as $$t$$ increases from $$\alpha$$ to $$\beta$$ . If $$C$$ is rotated about the $$x$$ -axis, then the area of the resulting surface is given by
$$S = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{2\pi y\sqrt{\left( \frac{\mathit{dx}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dt}} \right)^{2}}dt}}$$
The general symbolic formulas $$S = {\int{2\pi yds}}$$ and $$S = {\int{2\pi xds}}$$ (Formulas 8.2.7 and 8.2.8) are still valid, where $$\mathit{ds}$$ is given by Formula 6.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Show that the surface area of a sphere of radius $$r$$ is $$4\pi r^{2}$$ .
Solution The sphere is obtained by rotating the semicircle
$$x = r\cos t y = r\sin t 0 \leqslant t \leqslant \pi$$
about the $$x$$ -axis. Therefore, from Formula 9, we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {S = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{2\pi r\sin t\sqrt{{( - r\sin t)}^{2} + {({r\cos t})}^{2}}dt}}} \\ {\phantom{S} = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{\pi}{r\sin t\sqrt{r^{2}(\sin^{2}t + \cos^{2}t)}dt}} = 2\pi{\int_{0}^{\pi}{r\sin t \cdot rdt}}} \\ {\phantom{S} = 2\pi r^{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin tdt}} = 2\pi r^{2}( - \cos t)\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = 4\pi r^{2}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Applied Project Bézier Curves
section.paragraph: Bézier curves are used in computer-aided design (CAD) and are named after the French mathematician Pierre Bézier (1910–1999), who worked in the automotive industry. A cubic Bézier curve is determined by four control points, $$P_{0}(x_{0},y_{0})$$ , $$P_{1}(x_{1},y_{1})$$ , $$P_{2}(x_{2},y_{2})$$ , and $$P_{3}(x_{3},y_{3})$$ , and is defined by the parametric equations

where $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1$$ . Notice that when $$t = 0$$ we have $${({x,y})} = {({x_{0},y_{0}})}$$ and when $$t = 1$$ we have $${({x,y})} = {({x_{3},y_{3}})}$$ , so the curve starts at $$P_{0}$$ and ends at $$P_{3}$$ .

list.item: Graph the Bézier curve with control points $$P_{0}({4,1})$$ , $$P_{1}({28,48})$$ , $$P_{2}({50,42})$$ , and $$P_{3}({40,5})$$ . Then, on the same screen, graph the line segments $$P_{0}P_{1}$$ , $$P_{1}P_{2}$$ , and $$P_{2}P_{3}$$ . (Exercise 10.1.37 shows how to do this.) Notice that the middle control points $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ don’t lie on the curve; the curve starts at $$P_{0}$$ , heads toward $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ without reaching them, and ends at $$P_{3}$$ .
From the graph in Problem 1, it appears that the tangent at $$P_{0}$$ passes through $$P_{1}$$ and the tangent at $$P_{3}$$ passes through $$P_{2}$$ . Prove it.
Try to produce a Bézier curve with a loop by changing the second control point in Problem 1.
Some laser printers use Bézier curves to represent letters and other symbols. Experiment with control points until you find a Bézier curve that gives a reasonable representation of the letter C.

More complicated shapes can be represented by piecing together two or more Bézier curves. Suppose the first Bézier curve has control points $$P_{0}$$ , $$P_{1}$$ , $$P_{2}$$ , $$P_{3}$$ and the second one has control points $$P_{3}$$ , $$P_{4}$$ , $$P_{5}$$ , $$P_{6}$$ . If we want these two pieces to join together smoothly, then the tangents at $$P_{3}$$ should match and so the points $$P_{2}$$ , $$P_{3}$$ , and $$P_{4}$$ all have to lie on this common tangent line. Using this principle, find control points for a pair of Bézier curves that represent the letter S.
